claim: Edema stemming from leaky blood vessels is common in eye diseases such as age-related macular degeneration and diabetic retinopathy.
source: Edema stemming from leaky blood vessels is common in eye diseases such as age-related macular degeneration and diabetic retinopathy.
evidence: This is a statement of established medical knowledge about eye diseases.

claim: Therapies targeting vascular endothelial growth factor A (VEGFA) can suppress leakage.
source: Whereas therapies targeting vascular endothelial growth factor A (VEGFA) can suppress leakage, side-effects include vascular rarefaction and geographic atrophy.
evidence: This is established knowledge about VEGFA-targeting therapies.

claim: Side-effects of VEGFA-targeting therapies include vascular rarefaction and geographic atrophy.
source: Whereas therapies targeting vascular endothelial growth factor A (VEGFA) can suppress leakage, side-effects include vascular rarefaction and geographic atrophy.
evidence: This is established knowledge about side effects of VEGFA therapies.

claim: Targeting signaling downstream of VEGFR2 pY949 limits vascular permeability in retinopathy induced by high oxygen.
source: By challenging mouse models representing different steps in VEGFA/VEGF receptor 2 (VEGFR2)-induced vascular permeability, we show that targeting signaling downstream of VEGFR2 pY949 limits vascular permeability in retinopathy induced by high oxygen or by laser-wounding.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mouse models presented in the manuscript.

claim: Targeting signaling downstream of VEGFR2 pY949 limits vascular permeability in retinopathy induced by laser-wounding.
source: By challenging mouse models representing different steps in VEGFA/VEGF receptor 2 (VEGFR2)-induced vascular permeability, we show that targeting signaling downstream of VEGFR2 pY949 limits vascular permeability in retinopathy induced by high oxygen or by laser-wounding.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from mouse models presented in the manuscript.

claim: Suppressed permeability is accompanied by reduced pathological neoangiogenesis in oxygen-induced retinopathy.
source: Although suppressed permeability is accompanied by reduced pathological neoangiogenesis in oxygen-induced retinopathy, similarly sized lesions leak less in mutant mice, separating regulation of permeability from angiogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observations in the OIR model.

claim: Similarly sized lesions leak less in mutant mice, separating regulation of permeability from angiogenesis.
source: Although suppressed permeability is accompanied by reduced pathological neoangiogenesis in oxygen-induced retinopathy, similarly sized lesions leak less in mutant mice, separating regulation of permeability from angiogenesis.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing lesion size and leakage in mutant versus wild-type mice.

claim: VE-cadherin phosphorylation at the Y685 residue is reduced when VEGFR2 pY949 signaling is impaired.
source: Strikingly, vascular endothelial (VE)-cadherin phosphorylation at the Y685, but not Y658, residue is reduced when VEGFR2 pY949 signaling is impaired.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data presented in the manuscript.

claim: VE-cadherin phosphorylation at the Y658 residue is not reduced when VEGFR2 pY949 signaling is impaired.
source: Strikingly, vascular endothelial (VE)-cadherin phosphorylation at the Y685, but not Y658, residue is reduced when VEGFR2 pY949 signaling is impaired.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data presented in the manuscript.

claim: VE-cadherin Y685 phosphorylation is selectively associated with excessive vascular leakage.
source: These findings support a mechanism whereby VE-cadherin Y685 phosphorylation is selectively associated with excessive vascular leakage.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on VE-cadherin phosphorylation and leakage.

claim: Targeting VEGFR2-regulated VE-cadherin phosphorylation could suppress edema while leaving other VEGFR2-dependent functions intact.
source: Therapeutically, targeting VEGFR2-regulated VE-cadherin phosphorylation could suppress edema while leaving other VEGFR2-dependent functions intact.
evidence: This is a speculative therapeutic implication based on the experimental findings.

claim: Blood vessel dysfunction in the retina is a critical component of several blinding eye diseases.
source: Blood vessel dysfunction in the retina is a critical component of several blinding eye diseases.
evidence: This is established medical knowledge.

claim: The retina is sensitive to fluid accumulation that can result from excessively leaking blood vessels in the eye.
source: In particular, the retina is sensitive to the fluid accumulation that can result from excessively leaking blood vessels in the eye and reduction of the ensuing edema is a therapeutic goal in the clinic (Daruich et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Daruich et al., 2018.

claim: Reduction of edema is a therapeutic goal in the clinic.
source: In particular, the retina is sensitive to the fluid accumulation that can result from excessively leaking blood vessels in the eye and reduction of the ensuing edema is a therapeutic goal in the clinic (Daruich et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Daruich et al., 2018.

claim: VEGFA is one of the key factors controlling endothelial cell biology in the eye.
source: Vascular endothelial growth factor A (VEGFA) is one of the key factors controlling endothelial cell biology in the eye (Daruich et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Daruich et al., 2018.

claim: The importance of VEGFA signaling is underscored by the clinical success of antibodies neutralizing VEGFA.
source: The importance of VEGFA signaling is underscored by the clinical success of antibodies (bevacizumab, ranibizumab) neutralizing VEGFA, or soluble receptor fusion proteins (aflibercept), neutralizing several VEGF family members.
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about anti-VEGFA therapies.

claim: Anti-VEGFA drugs preserve vision in many patients.
source: These drugs preserve vision in many patients, but over time disease progression may resume, and for others there is no benefit even from the initial anti-VEGF treatment (Bressler et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bressler et al., 2017.

claim: Over time disease progression may resume in patients treated with anti-VEGFA drugs.
source: These drugs preserve vision in many patients, but over time disease progression may resume, and for others there is no benefit even from the initial anti-VEGF treatment (Bressler et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bressler et al., 2017.

claim: For some patients there is no benefit even from the initial anti-VEGF treatment.
source: These drugs preserve vision in many patients, but over time disease progression may resume, and for others there is no benefit even from the initial anti-VEGF treatment (Bressler et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bressler et al., 2017.

claim: VEGFA serves as a survival factor for VEGFR2-expressing retinal neurons.
source: The role of VEGFA for survival of VEGFR2-expressing retinal neurons presents an additional challenge (Nishijima et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Nishijima et al., 2007.

claim: Anti-VEGF treatment has been linked to capillary loss and rarefaction of normal adult vasculature.
source: Moreover, anti-VEGF treatment has been linked to capillary loss and rarefaction of normal adult vasculature (Kamba and McDonald, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Kamba and McDonald, 2007.

claim: The detrimental effects of long-lasting VEGFA suppression are now being recognized.
source: While a focus in the development of new therapies to treat retinopathies has been on increasing the potency of anti-VEGFA therapy, the detrimental effects of long-lasting VEGFA suppression are now being recognized (Usui-Ouchi and Friedlander, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Usui-Ouchi and Friedlander, 2019.

claim: The development of alternative treatments to block excessive vascular leakage in the eye while sparing other VEGF functions is very important.
source: Taken together, the development of alternative treatments to block excessive vascular leakage in the eye while sparing other VEGF functions is very important.
evidence: This is an inference based on the limitations of current therapies discussed in the manuscript.

claim: The retina is protected by a blood retinal barrier (BRB).
source: The retina is protected by a blood retinal barrier (BRB) which, under normal conditions, limits the extravasation of blood components into the tissue.
evidence: This is established anatomical and physiological knowledge.

claim: Under normal conditions, the BRB limits the extravasation of blood components into the tissue.
source: The retina is protected by a blood retinal barrier (BRB) which, under normal conditions, limits the extravasation of blood components into the tissue.
evidence: This is established physiological knowledge.

claim: The BRB consists of an inner barrier at the level of retinal vessels and an outer barrier at the cell junctions of the retinal pigment epithelium.
source: The BRB consists of an inner barrier at the level of retinal vessels and an outer barrier at the cell junctions of the retinal pigment epithelium and it serves to stringently protect the tissue from pathogens, edema and inflammation (Zhao et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhao et al., 2015.

claim: The BRB serves to stringently protect the tissue from pathogens, edema and inflammation.
source: The BRB consists of an inner barrier at the level of retinal vessels and an outer barrier at the cell junctions of the retinal pigment epithelium and it serves to stringently protect the tissue from pathogens, edema and inflammation (Zhao et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhao et al., 2015.

claim: The BRB is established in conjunction with vessel entry in the central nervous system during early development.
source: The BRB is established in conjunction with vessel entry in the central nervous system during early development (Chow and Gu, 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chow and Gu, 2017.

claim: In diabetic retinopathy, hypoxia and increased production of VEGFA is accompanied by breakdown of the BRB.
source: In eye diseases such as diabetic retinopathy, hypoxia and the ensuing increased production of VEGFA is accompanied by breakdown of the BRB (Campochiaro, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Campochiaro, 2015.

claim: The molecular mechanisms downstream of VEGFA leading to BRB disruption have not been defined.
source: The molecular mechanisms downstream of VEGFA leading to this disruption have not been defined.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: VEGFA was originally identified as vascular permeability factor (VPF).
source: VEGFA, originally identified as vascular permeability factor (VPF) (Senger et al., 1986), binds to VEGFR2 inducing receptor phosphorylation and the propagation of signaling cascades regulating endothelial survival, proliferation and motility (Simons et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Senger et al., 1986.

claim: VEGFA binds to VEGFR2 inducing receptor phosphorylation and the propagation of signaling cascades regulating endothelial survival, proliferation and motility.
source: VEGFA, originally identified as vascular permeability factor (VPF) (Senger et al., 1986), binds to VEGFR2 inducing receptor phosphorylation and the propagation of signaling cascades regulating endothelial survival, proliferation and motility (Simons et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Simons et al., 2016.

claim: Acute responses to VEGFR2 activity include destabilization of endothelial junctions leading to increased permeability.
source: Acute responses to VEGFR2 activity include destabilization of endothelial junctions leading to increased permeability.
evidence: This is established knowledge about VEGFR2 signaling.

claim: Phosphorylation of VEGFR2 at Y949 enhances permeability via the disruption of adherens junctions in the dermal vasculature.
source: Notably, phosphorylation of VEGFR2 at Y949 (951 in human) enhances permeability via the disruption of adherens junctions in the dermal vasculature, but also in pathologies such as neuroendocrine cancer, melanoma and glioblastoma (Li et al., 2016a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Li et al., 2016a.

claim: Phosphorylation of VEGFR2 at Y949 enhances permeability in pathologies such as neuroendocrine cancer, melanoma and glioblastoma.
source: Notably, phosphorylation of VEGFR2 at Y949 (951 in human) enhances permeability via the disruption of adherens junctions in the dermal vasculature, but also in pathologies such as neuroendocrine cancer, melanoma and glioblastoma (Li et al., 2016a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Li et al., 2016a.

claim: Phosphorylation of Y949 creates a binding site for the adaptor molecule T cell specific adaptor (TSAd).
source: Phosphorylation of Y949 creates a binding site for the adaptor molecule T cell specific adaptor (TSAd), which in turn binds c-Src at endothelial junctions (Li et al., 2016a; Matsumoto et al., 2005; Sun et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Li et al., 2016a; Matsumoto et al., 2005; Sun et al., 2012.

claim: TSAd binds c-Src at endothelial junctions.
source: Phosphorylation of Y949 creates a binding site for the adaptor molecule T cell specific adaptor (TSAd), which in turn binds c-Src at endothelial junctions (Li et al., 2016a; Matsumoto et al., 2005; Sun et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Li et al., 2016a; Matsumoto et al., 2005; Sun et al., 2012.

claim: c-Src is implicated in phosphorylation of vascular endothelial (VE)-cadherin.
source: c-Src is implicated in phosphorylation of vascular endothelial (VE)-cadherin (Li et al., 2016a; Adam et al., 2010; Vestweber, 2008; Wallez et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Li et al., 2016a; Adam et al., 2010; Vestweber, 2008; Wallez et al., 2007.

claim: VE-cadherin is the main component of endothelial adherens junctions.
source: VE-cadherin is the main component of endothelial adherens junctions, forming homophilic interactions between endothelial cells, and is critical in regulation of permeability in response to VEGFA as well as inflammatory cytokines (Li et al., 2016a; Akla et al., 2018; Lampugnani et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Li et al., 2016a; Akla et al., 2018; Lampugnani et al., 2018.

claim: VE-cadherin forms homophilic interactions between endothelial cells.
source: VE-cadherin is the main component of endothelial adherens junctions, forming homophilic interactions between endothelial cells, and is critical in regulation of permeability in response to VEGFA as well as inflammatory cytokines (Li et al., 2016a; Akla et al., 2018; Lampugnani et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Li et al., 2016a; Akla et al., 2018; Lampugnani et al., 2018.

claim: VE-cadherin is critical in regulation of permeability in response to VEGFA.
source: VE-cadherin is the main component of endothelial adherens junctions, forming homophilic interactions between endothelial cells, and is critical in regulation of permeability in response to VEGFA as well as inflammatory cytokines (Li et al., 2016a; Akla et al., 2018; Lampugnani et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Li et al., 2016a; Akla et al., 2018; Lampugnani et al., 2018.

evidence: This is supported by citations to Li et al., 2016a; Akla et al., 2018; Lampugnani et al., 2018.

claim: Tyrosine phosphorylation of VE-cadherin is associated with different biological functions.
source: Tyrosine phosphorylation of VE-cadherin is associated with different biological functions.
evidence: This is established knowledge about VE-cadherin regulation.

claim: Phosphorylation of VE-cadherin Y658 and Y685 is associated with the control of vascular permeability.
source: Thus, phosphorylation of Y658 and Y685 is associated with the control of vascular permeability (Orsenigo et al., 2012), and angiogenic sprouting (Gordon et al., 2016), and Y658 with junction stability (Garrett et al., 2017; Schulte et al., 2011), whereas phosphorylation of Y731 in VE-cadherin is linked to leukocyte extravasation (Wessel et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Orsenigo et al., 2012.

claim: Phosphorylation of VE-cadherin Y658 and Y685 is associated with angiogenic sprouting.
source: Thus, phosphorylation of Y658 and Y685 is associated with the control of vascular permeability (Orsenigo et al., 2012), and angiogenic sprouting (Gordon et al., 2016), and Y658 with junction stability (Garrett et al., 2017; Schulte et al., 2011), whereas phosphorylation of Y731 in VE-cadherin is linked to leukocyte extravasation (Wessel et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gordon et al., 2016.

claim: Phosphorylation of VE-cadherin Y658 is associated with junction stability.
source: Thus, phosphorylation of Y658 and Y685 is associated with the control of vascular permeability (Orsenigo et al., 2012), and angiogenic sprouting (Gordon et al., 2016), and Y658 with junction stability (Garrett et al., 2017; Schulte et al., 2011), whereas phosphorylation of Y731 in VE-cadherin is linked to leukocyte extravasation (Wessel et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Garrett et al., 2017; Schulte et al., 2011.

claim: Phosphorylation of VE-cadherin Y731 is linked to leukocyte extravasation.
source: Thus, phosphorylation of Y658 and Y685 is associated with the control of vascular permeability (Orsenigo et al., 2012), and angiogenic sprouting (Gordon et al., 2016), and Y658 with junction stability (Garrett et al., 2017; Schulte et al., 2011), whereas phosphorylation of Y731 in VE-cadherin is linked to leukocyte extravasation (Wessel et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wessel et al., 2014.

claim: Serine phosphorylation of VE-cadherin at S665 is implicated in regulation of endothelial junctions.
source: Serine phosphorylation of VE-cadherin at S665 is also implicated in regulation of endothelial junctions (Gavard and Gutkind, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gavard and Gutkind, 2006.

claim: KdrY949F/Y949F mice exhibit suppressed vessel permeability in the dermis specifically in response to VEGFA.
source: We have previously shown that KdrY949F/Y949F exhibits suppressed vessel permeability in the dermis specifically in response to VEGFA (Li et al., 2016a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Li et al., 2016a.

claim: The stringent BRB of the retinal vasculature is not expected to be regulated by VEGFA under normal conditions.
source: The stringent BRB of the retinal vasculature is not expected to be regulated by VEGFA, however, in ocular disease such as retinopathy, the BRB may be broken down (Urias et al., 2017); in accordance, proliferative retinopathies are characterized by increased transvessel flow and edema (Campochiaro, 2015; Kim et al., 2016; Luo et al., 2011; Stahl et al., 2010a).
evidence: This is an inference based on established knowledge and cited literature.

claim: In ocular disease such as retinopathy, the BRB may be broken down.
source: The stringent BRB of the retinal vasculature is not expected to be regulated by VEGFA, however, in ocular disease such as retinopathy, the BRB may be broken down (Urias et al., 2017); in accordance, proliferative retinopathies are characterized by increased transvessel flow and edema (Campochiaro, 2015; Kim et al., 2016; Luo et al., 2011; Stahl et al., 2010a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Urias et al., 2017.

claim: Proliferative retinopathies are characterized by increased transvessel flow and edema.
source: The stringent BRB of the retinal vasculature is not expected to be regulated by VEGFA, however, in ocular disease such as retinopathy, the BRB may be broken down (Urias et al., 2017); in accordance, proliferative retinopathies are characterized by increased transvessel flow and edema (Campochiaro, 2015; Kim et al., 2016; Luo et al., 2011; Stahl et al., 2010a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Campochiaro, 2015; Kim et al., 2016; Luo et al., 2011; Stahl et al., 2010a.

claim: Laser-induced choroidal neovascularization (CNV) lesions mimic the progression of exudative age-related macular degeneration.
source: The vascular lesions established after laser pulse disruption of the Bruch's membrane mimic the progression of exudative age-related macular degeneration (Lambert et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lambert et al., 2013.

claim: CNV lesions develop from the choroidal vessels over the course of several days as a consequence of hypoxia and elevated production of VEGFA.
source: The lesions develop from the choroidal vessels over the course of several days as a consequence of hypoxia and elevated production of VEGFA (André et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to André et al., 2015.

claim: CNV lesions were of equal size between KdrY949F/Y949F and Kdr+/+ mice at day 14.
source: Lesions were of equal size (Figure 1A–B; 42038 µm2 ± 2514, Kdr+/+; 44399 µm2 ± 3454, KdrY949F/Y949F), still, microsphere accumulation was significantly reduced in the vicinity of KdrY949F/Y949F lesions as compared to the Kdr+/+ lesions (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1A-B.

claim: Microsphere accumulation was significantly reduced in the vicinity of KdrY949F/Y949F CNV lesions compared to Kdr+/+ lesions.
source: Lesions were of equal size (Figure 1A–B; 42038 µm2 ± 2514, Kdr+/+; 44399 µm2 ± 3454, KdrY949F/Y949F), still, microsphere accumulation was significantly reduced in the vicinity of KdrY949F/Y949F lesions as compared to the Kdr+/+ lesions (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1C-D.

claim: Pathological leakage in the choroid can be suppressed by attenuation of pY949 VEGFR2 signaling.
source: We conclude that pathological leakage in the choroid can be suppressed by attenutation of pY949 VEGFR2 signaling and that this decrease is not simply due to an anti-angiogenic effect of interrupted VEGFA signaling.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the CNV experimental data.

claim: The decrease in leakage in KdrY949F/Y949F mice is not simply due to an anti-angiogenic effect of interrupted VEGFA signaling.
source: We conclude that pathological leakage in the choroid can be suppressed by attenutation of pY949 VEGFR2 signaling and that this decrease is not simply due to an anti-angiogenic effect of interrupted VEGFA signaling.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that lesion sizes were equal but leakage was reduced.

claim: In the OIR model, mice are exposed to 75% oxygen during postnatal days 7-12.
source: In the OIR model, mice are exposed to 75% oxygen during postnatal (P) days 7–12 after which they are returned to normal atmosphere (21% oxygen).
evidence: This describes the experimental protocol used.

claim: During the first stage of OIR, VEGFA expression is suppressed which leads to apoptosis of capillaries in the central region of the retina.
source: During the first stage, VEGFA expression is suppressed which leads to apoptosis of capillaries in the central region of the retina (Lange et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Lange et al., 2009.

claim: In the second stage of OIR, retinal VEGFA expression is induced as a consequence of moving mice from high oxygen to normal atmosphere.
source: In the second stage, retinal VEGFA expression is induced as a consequence of moving mice from high oxygen to normal atmosphere (relative hypoxia), leading to the formation of pathological neovascular tufts, characterized by being disorganized and leaky (Connor et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Connor et al., 2009.

claim: The second stage of OIR leads to the formation of pathological neovascular tufts, characterized by being disorganized and leaky.
source: In the second stage, retinal VEGFA expression is induced as a consequence of moving mice from high oxygen to normal atmosphere (relative hypoxia), leading to the formation of pathological neovascular tufts, characterized by being disorganized and leaky (Connor et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Connor et al., 2009.

claim: At P17, KdrY949F/Y949F mice had a reduction in tuft formation compared to Kdr+/+ mice.
source: Of note, at P17, KdrY949F/Y949F mice had a reduction in tuft formation compared to the Kdr+/+ mice (Figure 2A–C; see Figure 2—figure supplement 1A for images without overlay).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2A-C.

claim: The reduced tuft formation in KdrY949F/Y949F mice was not due to differences in body weight of P17 pups.
source: This was not due to differences in body weight of P17 pups (Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Table 1.

claim: The reduced tuft formation was a result of suppressed pathological angiogenesis during the P12-17 period.
source: The reduced tuft formation was a result of suppressed pathological angiogenesis during the P12-17 period when mice were kept in normal atmosphere following the hyperoxia period.
evidence: This is an inference based on the timing of tuft formation.

claim: At P12, the morphology of the retina vasculature was similar for KdrY949F/Y949F and Kdr+/+ littermates.
source: At P12, the morphology of the retina vasculature was similar for KdrY949F/Y949F and Kdr+/+ littermates (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–C.

claim: Extravascular accumulation of microspheres in regions of neovascular tuft growth was significantly suppressed in KdrY949F/Y949F retinas compared to Kdr+/+.
source: Importantly, extravascular accumulation of microspheres in regions of neovascular tuft growth was significantly suppressed in KdrY949F/Y949F retinas compared to Kdr+/+ (Figure 2D–E).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2D-E.

claim: Disrupting pY949 signaling during OIR leads to a suppression of pathological vessel leakage.
source: We conclude that disrupting pY949 signaling during OIR leads to a suppression of pathological vessel leakage and also to a reduction in pathological neoangiogenesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the OIR experimental data.

claim: Disrupting pY949 signaling during OIR leads to a reduction in pathological neoangiogenesis.
source: We conclude that disrupting pY949 signaling during OIR leads to a suppression of pathological vessel leakage and also to a reduction in pathological neoangiogenesis.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the OIR experimental data.

claim: Remaining tufts leaked less in OIR-challenged KdrY949F/Y949F mice.
source: The decrease in tuft formation in itself results in reduced overall leakage, however, it should be noted that remaining tufts leaked less in OIR-challenged KdrY949F/Y949F mice (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The extent of infiltration of inflammatory CD68+ and CD45+ cells were similar at P17 for the KdrY949F/Y949F and Kdr+/+ strains.
source: Moreover, the extent of infiltration of inflammatory CD68+ and CD45+ cells were similar at P17 for the KdrY949F/Y949F and Kdr+/+ strains indicating that the enhanced barrier in the KdrY949F/Y949F pups was specific for macromolecules and did not exclude inflammatory cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–C.

claim: The enhanced barrier in the KdrY949F/Y949F pups was specific for macromolecules and did not exclude inflammatory cells.
source: Moreover, the extent of infiltration of inflammatory CD68+ and CD45+ cells were similar at P17 for the KdrY949F/Y949F and Kdr+/+ strains indicating that the enhanced barrier in the KdrY949F/Y949F pups was specific for macromolecules and did not exclude inflammatory cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the inflammatory cell infiltration data.

claim: TSAd binds to pY949 with high affinity.
source: The canonical signalling pathway downstream of the pY949 phosphosite consists of the Src Homology 2 (SH2) containing adaptor-protein TSAd (gene designation Sh2d2a), which binds to pY949 with high affinity.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the TSAd-VEGFR2 interaction.

claim: TSAd recruits c-Src, leading to the phosphorylation of VE-cadherin.
source: TSAd in turn recruits c-Src, leading to the phosphorylation of VE-cadherin (illustrated in Figure 3A; Li et al., 2016a; Sun et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Li et al., 2016a; Sun et al., 2012 and illustrated in Figure 3A.

claim: Tuft formation was reduced in Sh2d2a iECKO mice to a similar extent as seen with KdrY949F/Y949F mice.
source: After OIR challenge of Sh2d2aiECKO mice along with their wild-type littermates (Sh2d2afl/fl; referred to as Sh2d2aiECWT), tuft formation was reduced in Sh2d2a iECKO mice to a similar extent as seen with KdrY949F/Y949F mice (Figure 3B–C: see Figure 3—figure supplement 1A for images without overlay) while the avascular area was similar in the Sh2d2aiECKO and Sh2d2aiECWT mice at P17 (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3B-C.

claim: The avascular area was similar in the Sh2d2aiECKO and Sh2d2aiECWT mice at P17.
source: After OIR challenge of Sh2d2aiECKO mice along with their wild-type littermates (Sh2d2afl/fl; referred to as Sh2d2aiECWT), tuft formation was reduced in Sh2d2a iECKO mice to a similar extent as seen with KdrY949F/Y949F mice (Figure 3B–C: see Figure 3—figure supplement 1A for images without overlay) while the avascular area was similar in the Sh2d2aiECKO and Sh2d2aiECWT mice at P17 (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Cre recombination in the Sh2d2aiECKO model was approximately 80% as assessed by vessel area.
source: Cre recombination in the Sh2d2aiECKO model was approximately 80% as assessed by vessel area (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C), in agreement with immunoblotting analysis performed earlier to show the efficiency of Sh2d2a excision in this model (Gordon et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B,C and citation to Gordon et al., 2016.

claim: The distribution of recombined endothelial cells was similar between neoangiogenic tufts and the normal vasculature.
source: The distribution of recombined endothelial cells was similar between neoangiogenic tufts and the normal vasculature.
evidence: This is an observation from the Sh2d2aiECKO model.

claim: c-Src phosphorylates VE-cadherin in vitro.
source: The cytoplasmic tyrosine kinase c-Src phosphorylates VE-cadherin in vitro (Adam et al., 2010; Orsenigo et al., 2012) and its activity correlates with detection of phosphorylated VE-cadherin in vivo (Orsenigo et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Adam et al., 2010; Orsenigo et al., 2012.

claim: c-Src activity correlates with detection of phosphorylated VE-cadherin in vivo.
source: The cytoplasmic tyrosine kinase c-Src phosphorylates VE-cadherin in vitro (Adam et al., 2010; Orsenigo et al., 2012) and its activity correlates with detection of phosphorylated VE-cadherin in vivo (Orsenigo et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Orsenigo et al., 2012.

claim: Neovascular tufts exhibited elevated levels of pY418 c-Src.
source: Immunostaining for pY418, a tyrosine residue in c-Src kinase domain required for maximal kinase activity, revealed active c-Src at the periphery of the retina and elevated levels in the neovascular tufts of KdrY949F/Y949F and Kdr+/+ mice (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Some pY418 c-Src immunostaining was localized at cell-cell junctions.
source: Of interest, some pY418 c-Src immunostaining was localized at cell-cell junctions as indicated by co-staining with VE-cadherin.
evidence: This is an observation from immunostaining experiments.

claim: The level of junctional pY418 c-Src was similar in tufts from KdrY949F/Y949F and Kdr+/+ mice.
source: Notably, the level of junctional pY418 c-Src was similar in tufts from KdrY949F/Y949F and Kdr+/+ mice (Figure 3F), indicating that pY949 signaling does not account for c-Src activity at cell-cell junctions in this model.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: pY949 signaling does not account for c-Src activity at cell-cell junctions in the retina vasculature.
source: Notably, the level of junctional pY418 c-Src was similar in tufts from KdrY949F/Y949F and Kdr+/+ mice (Figure 3F), indicating that pY949 signaling does not account for c-Src activity at cell-cell junctions in this model.

claim: Signaling through pY949 in VEGFR2 does not contribute to regulation of c-Src kinase activity at endothelial junctions in the retina vasculature.

claim: VE-cadherin is the major component of adherens junctions.

claim: VE-cadherin is vital for vessel integrity.

evidence: This is supported by citation to Giannotta et al., 2013.

claim: Neovascular tufts exhibited junctions with an irregular VE-cadherin morphology compared to non-tuft regions.

claim: Irregular VE-cadherin morphology in tufts is suggestive of increased internalization and degradation of VE-cadherin.

claim: Tuft endothelial junctions were detected by antibodies against pY658 and pY685 VE-cadherin.

claim: pY658 and pY685 VE-cadherin are associated with VE-cadherin turnover.
source: In agreement, tuft endothelial junctions were detected by antibodies against two known phosphorylation sites in VE-cadherin, pY658 and pY685 (Figure 3G,H), associated with VE-cadherin turnover (Orsenigo et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Orsenigo et al., 2012.

claim: The level of pY658 immunostaining was similar between KdrY949F/Y949F and Kdr+/+ tufts.

claim: pY685 levels were significantly lower in the KdrY949F/Y949F retinal tufts compared to Kdr+/+.

claim: Arteries throughout the retina essentially lacked immunostaining for pY685 and pY658.

claim: CNV lesions at D14 displayed pY685 VE-cadherin immunostaining.

claim: The intensity of the pY685 signal was significantly lower in the KdrY949F/Y949F CNV lesions.

evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: Junctional VE-cadherin phosphorylation at Y685 is dependent on pY949 VEGFR2 signaling in the choroid vasculature.
source: This result suggests that junctional VE-cadherin phosphorylation at Y685 is dependent on pY949 VEGFR2 signaling also in the choroid vasculature.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the pY685 immunostaining data in CNV lesions.

claim: Tuft formation was reduced in VEC-Y685F pups compared to VEC-WT controls at P17.

claim: The avascular area after high oxygen-exposure was equivalent between VEC-Y685F and VEC-WT mice.
source: As for the KdrY949F/Y949F and Sh2d2aiECKO strains strains, the avascular area after high oxygen-exposure was equivalent between VEC-Y685F and VEC-WT mice (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: There was no difference in the levels of total VE-cadherin in the VEC-Y685F tufts compared to WT.

claim: There was no difference in the levels of VE-cadherin pY658 in the VEC-Y685F tufts compared to WT.
source: There was no difference in the levels of total VE-cadherin or VE-cadherin pY658 detected by immunostaining, in the VEC-Y685F tufts compared to WT (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: Microsphere accumulation was significantly reduced in the tufts of VEC-Y685F mice following OIR, compared to VEC-WT.

claim: Microsphere leakage was similar in VEC-WT and littermate C57Bl/6 P17 mice after OIR.

evidence: This is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1G–H.

claim: VEGFR2 and downstream VE-cadherin Y685 phosphorylation play an essential role in elevated vascular leakage in retinopathies.
source: Combined, these data show an essential role for VEGFR2 and downstream VE-cadherin Y685 phosphorylation in elevated vascular leakage in retinopathies.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the combined experimental data.

claim: Blocking VEGFA-induced VEGFR2 pY949 signaling at any of several steps in the downstream pathway leads to reduced vascular leakage in OIR.
source: Here we demonstrate that blocking VEGFA-induced VEGFR2 pY949 signaling at any of several steps in the downstream pathway, leads to reduced vascular leakage in two independent retinopathy models, OIR and CNV.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: Blocking VEGFA-induced VEGFR2 pY949 signaling at any of several steps in the downstream pathway leads to reduced vascular leakage in CNV.
source: Here we demonstrate that blocking VEGFA-induced VEGFR2 pY949 signaling at any of several steps in the downstream pathway, leads to reduced vascular leakage in two independent retinopathy models, OIR and CNV.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: Exposure to high oxygen in the OIR procedure causes pathological vascularization in the superficial retinal vessels.
source: While exposure to high oxygen in the OIR procedure causes pathological vascularization in the superficial retinal vessels, the CNV laser injury targets the choroidal vasculature.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the OIR model.

claim: The CNV laser injury targets the choroidal vasculature.
source: While exposure to high oxygen in the OIR procedure causes pathological vascularization in the superficial retinal vessels, the CNV laser injury targets the choroidal vasculature.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the CNV model.

claim: VEGFR2 pY949 signaling is implicated in exaggerated vascular leakage in two very different vascular beds in the retina.
source: Thus, we implicate VEGFR2 pY949 signaling in exaggerated vascular leakage in two very different vascular beds in the retina.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in both OIR and CNV models.

claim: Components of the VEGFR2 pY949 signaling axis can be targeted to control excessive vascular leakage and pathological neoangiogenesis without interfering with physiological functions of VEGFA.
source: Importantly, we identify components of a signaling axis that can be targeted in order to control excessive vascular leakage and pathological neoangiogenesis without interfering with physiological functions of VEGFA.
evidence: This is a conclusion and therapeutic implication drawn from the experimental data.

claim: Pathological vascular tuft formation was diminished in the KdrY949F/Y949F strain.
source: Although pathological vascular tuft formation was diminished in the KdrY949F/Y949F strain, careful characterization of the vasculature in different organs of this strain has not revealed deficiencies in vessel density or morphology during development (Li et al., 2016a).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and citation to Li et al., 2016a.

claim: Careful characterization of the vasculature in different organs of the KdrY949F/Y949F strain has not revealed deficiencies in vessel density or morphology during development.
source: Although pathological vascular tuft formation was diminished in the KdrY949F/Y949F strain, careful characterization of the vasculature in different organs of this strain has not revealed deficiencies in vessel density or morphology during development (Li et al., 2016a).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Li et al., 2016a.

claim: The improved barrier properties in the KdrY949F/Y949F vasculature do not exclude infiltration of CD68/CD45+ inflammatory cells.
source: Of note, the improved barrier properties in the KdrY949F/Y949F vasculature do not exclude infiltration of CD68/CD45+ inflammatory cells (Li et al., 2016a and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Li et al., 2016a and data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Suppressed macromolecular leakage in response to VEGFA plays an important role in pathologies while it is dispensable in physiology.
source: Nevertheless, based on the currently available information, we favor the notion that suppressed macromolecular leakage in response to VEGFA plays an important role in pathologies while it is dispensable in physiology.
evidence: This is an inference and interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Leakage suppression may to some extent interfere with neoangiogenesis due to the lack of a fibrinogen mesh for the new vessel to grow on.
source: We do not exclude that leakage suppression to some extent interferes with neoangiogenesis due to the lack of a fibrinogen mesh for the new vessel to grow on Dvorak et al. (1995).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by citation to Dvorak et al. (1995).

claim: Leakage was suppressed in the KdrY949F/Y949F retinas in both the CNV and OIR models when normalized to neovascular area.
source: However, as leakage was suppressed in the KdrY949F/Y949F retinas in both the CNV and OIR (normalized to neovascular area) models, our data support the concept that leakage is regulated separately from angiogenesis per se.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from both models.

claim: Leakage is regulated separately from angiogenesis per se.
source: However, as leakage was suppressed in the KdrY949F/Y949F retinas in both the CNV and OIR (normalized to neovascular area) models, our data support the concept that leakage is regulated separately from angiogenesis per se.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: In a range of tissues, either in the CNS or in peripheral organs, the VEGFR2 – TSAd – VE-cadherin pathway regulates vascular leakage in the context of disease, independent of angiogenesis.
source: We conclude that in a range of tissues, either in the CNS or in peripheral organs, the VEGFR2 – TSAd – VE-cadherin pathway regulates vascular leakage in the context of disease, independent of angiogenesis.
evidence: This is a broad conclusion drawn from the experimental data and previous studies.

claim: Using intravenously injected microspheres to assess leakage allows addressing both pathological vessel growth and leakage simultaneously.
source: A considerable strength of our study is in the use of intravenously injected microspheres to assess leakage, as we are able to address both pathological vessel growth and leakage simultaneously.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the study design.

claim: The microsphere methodology is superior to traditional methodologies using Evans blue injection.
source: This is superior to traditional methodologies using Evans blue injection, to determine the area of dye leakage over the retina surface, or measure the relative amount of dye extracted from retinas using formamide (Xu et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a methodological comparison supported by citation to Xu et al., 2001.

claim: The microsphere methodology allows for the precise visualization of the leakage and how it relates to vessel morphology.
source: Unlike the methodology described here, neither of these methods allow for the precise visualization of the leakage or how it relates to vessel morphology.
evidence: This is a methodological statement about the advantages of the microsphere approach.

claim: A complete loss of VEGFA-induced signaling in the eye can lead to atrophy of the neural layers in rodent models.
source: Studies in rodent models have suggested that a complete loss of VEGFA-induced signaling in the eye can lead to atrophy of the neural layers, which mechanistically can be explained by the presence of VEGFR2 on retinal neurons (Okabe et al., 2014; Saint-Geniez et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Okabe et al., 2014; Saint-Geniez et al., 2008.

claim: The presence of VEGFR2 on retinal neurons can mechanistically explain atrophy of neural layers following loss of VEGFA signaling.
source: Studies in rodent models have suggested that a complete loss of VEGFA-induced signaling in the eye can lead to atrophy of the neural layers, which mechanistically can be explained by the presence of VEGFR2 on retinal neurons (Okabe et al., 2014; Saint-Geniez et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Okabe et al., 2014; Saint-Geniez et al., 2008.

claim: In rats, anti-VEGFA treatment does not lead to damage of neural cells or loss of photoreceptor function.
source: In rats, anti-VEGFA treatment does not lead to damage of neural cells or loss of photoreceptor function (Long et al., 2018), indicating that VEGFA might indeed be dispensable for the neural retina in this species.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Long et al., 2018.

claim: VEGFA might be dispensable for the neural retina in rats.
source: In rats, anti-VEGFA treatment does not lead to damage of neural cells or loss of photoreceptor function (Long et al., 2018), indicating that VEGFA might indeed be dispensable for the neural retina in this species.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the rat study cited.

claim: Retrospective and long term follow-up studies in human patients treated with anti-VEGFA therapies provide examples of rare negative side effects such as hemorrhages.
source: However, retrospective and long term follow-up studies in human patients treated with anti-VEGFA therapies do provide examples of rare negative side effects such as hemorrhages, potentially linked to a systemic reduction of VEGFA (Avery, 2014; Falavarjani and Nguyen, 2013; Keir et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Avery, 2014; Falavarjani and Nguyen, 2013; Keir et al., 2017.

claim: Hemorrhages in anti-VEGFA treated patients are potentially linked to a systemic reduction of VEGFA.
source: However, retrospective and long term follow-up studies in human patients treated with anti-VEGFA therapies do provide examples of rare negative side effects such as hemorrhages, potentially linked to a systemic reduction of VEGFA (Avery, 2014; Falavarjani and Nguyen, 2013; Keir et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by citations.

claim: Anti-VEGFA treatment may contribute to the progression of geographic atrophy due to insufficient vascularization.
source: Furthermore, anti-VEGFA treatment may contribute to the progression of geographic atrophy due to insufficient vascularization or to the fact that VEGFA may serve as a vital survival factor for the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE) (Byeon et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by citation to Byeon et al., 2010.

claim: VEGFA may serve as a vital survival factor for the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE).

evidence: This is supported by citation to Byeon et al., 2010.

claim: Increased treatment frequency in patients receiving ranibizumab or bevacizumab is associated with greater loss of RPE.
source: Increased treatment frequency in patients receiving ranibizumab or bevacizumab is associated with greater loss of RPE, indicating geographic atrophy (Enslow et al., 2016; Grunwald et al., 2014; Rofagha et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Enslow et al., 2016; Grunwald et al., 2014; Rofagha et al., 2013.

claim: The necessity of repeated intraocular injections for the administration of current anti-VEGFA therapy reduces patient compliance.
source: The necessity of repeated intraocular injections (Patel et al., 2013) for the administration of current anti-VEGFA therapy reduces patient compliance (Polat et al., 2017) and results in rare but serious instances of eye damage caused by the injection procedure, such as endophthalmitis or retinal detachment (Falavarjani and Nguyen, 2013; Li et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Patel et al., 2013 and Polat et al., 2017.

claim: Repeated intraocular injections result in rare but serious instances of eye damage such as endophthalmitis or retinal detachment.
source: The necessity of repeated intraocular injections (Patel et al., 2013) for the administration of current anti-VEGFA therapy reduces patient compliance (Polat et al., 2017) and results in rare but serious instances of eye damage caused by the injection procedure, such as endophthalmitis or retinal detachment (Falavarjani and Nguyen, 2013; Li et al., 2016b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Falavarjani and Nguyen, 2013; Li et al., 2016b.

claim: The interaction between VEGFR2 pY949/pY951 and TSAd would be an ideal target to specifically block leakage but save other aspects of VEGFR2 biology.
source: Ultimately, the interaction between VEGFR2 pY949/pY951 and TSAd would be an ideal target to specifically block leakage but save other aspects of VEGFR2 biology.
evidence: This is a speculative therapeutic implication.

claim: Src family kinases (SFK) are implicated in the phosphorylation of tyrosine residues on VE-cadherin.
source: The literature strongly implicates Src family kinases (SFK) in the phosphorylation of tyrosine residues on VE-cadherin, thereby playing an essential role in controlling vessel permeability (Adam et al., 2010; Orsenigo et al., 2012; Wessel et al., 2014; Trani and Dejana, 2015).

evidence: This is supported by citations to Adam et al., 2010; Orsenigo et al., 2012; Wessel et al., 2014; Trani and Dejana, 2015.

evidence: This is supported by citations to Seo and Suh, 2017; Werdich and Penn, 2006.

claim: Indirect inhibition of c-Src kinase results in decreased tuft formation in the context of OIR.
source: In the context of OIR, direct inhibition of c-Src activation by kinase inhibitors (Seo and Suh, 2017; Werdich and Penn, 2006), indirect inhibition of c-Src kinase (Toutounchian et al., 2017), or suppressed c-Src expression using siRNA (Zhang et al., 2010), all result in decreased tuft formation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Toutounchian et al., 2017.

claim: Suppressed c-Src expression using siRNA results in decreased tuft formation in the context of OIR.
source: In the context of OIR, direct inhibition of c-Src activation by kinase inhibitors (Seo and Suh, 2017; Werdich and Penn, 2006), indirect inhibition of c-Src kinase (Toutounchian et al., 2017), or suppressed c-Src expression using siRNA (Zhang et al., 2010), all result in decreased tuft formation.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2010.

claim: While activation of c-Src alone may be required for induction of permeability and tuft formation, it may not be sufficient to induce these events.
source: These data indicate that while activation of c-Src alone may be required for induction of permeability and tuft formation, it may not be sufficient to induce these events.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data on c-Src activity.

claim: A triggering event, in addition to c-Src activity, is needed for opening of paracellular junctions.
source: In agreement, a triggering event, in addition to c-Src activity, is needed for opening of paracellular junctions (Adam et al., 2010; Adam et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Adam et al., 2010; Adam et al., 2016.

claim: Orsenigo and coworkers detected constitutive, flow-dependent pY418 c-Src in leakage-permissive venules.

evidence: This is supported by citation to Orsenigo et al., 2012.

claim: VEGFR2 pY949 signaling leads to close proximity and complex formation between VEGFR2 and VE-cadherin potentially involving c-Src.
source: Our data suggests the scenario that VEGFR2 pY949 signaling leads to close proximity and complex formation between VEGFR2 and VE-cadherin potentially involving c-Src (Li et al., 2016a), which may be activated in a VEGFR2-independent manner.

source: Our data suggests the scenario that VEGFR2 pY949 signaling leads to close proximity and complex formation between VEGFR2 and VE-cadherin potentially involving c-Src (Li et al., 2016a), which may be activated in a VEGFR2-independent manner.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the data.

evidence: This is a methodological caveat about antibody specificity.

source: Currently, reagents specifically recognizing only c-Src are missing.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of available research tools.

source: The acute stimulation of blood vessels with bradykinin or histamine to induce leakage is linked to a strong and transient drop in VE-cadherin phosphorylation due to internalization and degradation (Orsenigo et al., 2012).

claim: VE-cadherin pY685 is a key mediator in leakage regulation.

claim: Sites of leakage in a cremaster model correlated with staining for VE-cadherin pY685.

evidence: This is supported by citation to Wessel et al., 2014.

source: The mechanism underlying the important role of VE-cadherin pY685 compared to pY658 in vascular permeability is not understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge.

source: The pY685 phosphosite serves as the binding site for C-terminal Src Kinase (CSK), a negative regulator of c-Src activity.

source: CSK phosphorylates c-Src at pY527, leading to its inactivation (Latour and Veillette, 2001).

claim: CSK deletion in vitro does not alter barrier properties.

evidence: This is supported by citation to Adam et al., 2010.

source: Phosphorylation of the site acts to displace bound p120 catenin leading to destabilized adherens junctions (Garrett et al., 2017; Schulte et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Garrett et al., 2017; Schulte et al., 2011.

claim: Low levels of shear stress lead to maximal pY658 immunostaining.
